video.title: 5 TINY HABITS THAT MAKE YOU INSTANTLY LUCKIER (backed by psychology)

protocol.status: v2 labeler B (rubric v2), independent of A
protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Richard Wiseman spent 10 years studying self-described lucky and unlucky people, found four behaviors, then built a school teaching them to unlucky people; after one month they reported better opportunities and felt luckier (68.5). 'I'm being 100% serious' (72.7) is the latest acceptable end.

Two women in the same coffee shop: one with headphones in, one asks a stranger about a book -> coffee -> friendship -> job referral six months later. Payoff: she got lucky because of her proactive behavior (151.2).

How Wiseman proved lucky people notice more: count photos in a newspaper; unlucky people took two minutes, lucky people seconds - why? A huge message on page two said 'stop counting, there are 43', and a later one offered 250 pounds. Lucky people saw both; unlucky people kept counting (213.5).

Granovetter 1973: he expected people to find jobs through close friends and family, but over 80% did through someone they barely know - 'weak ties' (313.2). The surprising fact lands at 310.4; the 'why' (close ties share your opportunities, weak ties bridge to new ones) to 333.6 is also good - both edges genuinely work.

Stanford professor Tina Seelig, about to sleep on a flight to Ecuador, says hello to a stranger instead; years of follow-ups later it becomes a bestselling book deal. Payoff: people call it luck, but she said hello to a stranger she could have ignored (396.6). 'about this' in the opener points to weak ties but the story stands alone.

'Gut instincts, intuition - that sounds like woo-woo... but there's real science': your unconscious processes far more than your conscious mind and signals a recognised pattern before you can say why (489.3). Adding 'most of us override it with overthinking' and the party example to 508.0 also works.

1968 Pygmalion experiment: teachers told random kids were 'late bloomers'; by year's end they outperformed peers because teachers gave them harder work and more attention. Payoff: 'the expectation changed the behavior, and the behavior changed the outcome' (581.1).

Wiseman asks a lucky man in a leg cast if he still feels lucky; he says last time in hospital he met a nurse and they've been married 25 years. Then: unlucky people imagine how it could have been better, lucky people how it could have been worse - 'it could have been my neck' (671.0-672.2). The anecdote alone ends at 651.4, under the band.

also_ok.why: Fortune is what happens to you; luck is what you do about it. Crisp but just under the band.
Luck diary: write down small good things nightly; 'this is not just gratitude journaling' - you're telling your brain what to track, so you notice more opportunities. Practice-shaped.

negatives.why: Hook ('their luck is not random, it's a trainable skill') into the channel intro.
Weak-tie outreach practice; the quotable 'you cannot engineer good fortune' is a two-line button on the weak-ties section.
60-second rule practice; relies on the gut-instinct section before it.
Optimistic walking practice and 'bonus behavior' framing.
Wrap-up: 'luck surface area' restates the whole video.
